title: Grade 3 language, mean item-success rate - NAS and PARAKH

source.name: PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024 National Report (NCERT); NAS 2017 and NAS 2021 figures relayed via ASER 2018 and PIB

breaks.note: Instrument reset. NCERT states NAS 2017 is 'not comparable with earlier versions due to changes in sampling, test design, and content'; NAS 2021 changed the frame again (private unaided admitted, 720 districts, Class X added) and moved administration to CBSE. Not comparable with NAS 2017.

Instrument reset again. PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024 tests Grades III, VI and IX against NEP 2020 stage competencies rather than Grades III, V and VIII against RTE learning outcomes. PARAKH's stated position is that only Grade 3 survives across 2017, 2021 and 2024 - and PARAKH's own release then compares Grade 3 anyway, announcing gains. The caveat is deployed where the trend would look bad and set aside where it looks good.

points.note: NAS 2017. Government and government-aided schools only at elementary level; private unaided excluded entirely. T4 - nas.gov.in and ncert.nic.in do not resolve, so the figure is relayed, not retrieved.
NAS 2021. T4, relayed.
PARAKH 2024, T1 within a T4 series. Chance-corrected onto the 25-to-100 interval this is about 52 per cent; PARAKH publishes no chance-corrected score.

denominator: Test items presented, averaged over students enrolled in the sampled school section AND PRESENT ON TEST DAY. Absentees are replaced by present children under the sampling rule, so the realised sample is a probability sample of students present, not of students enrolled. Out-of-school children are outside the frame entirely.
caveat: NOT A TREND LINE. These three points are three different instruments wearing one name, each of which its own custodians say breaks comparison with its predecessor. India's official learning instrument has been reset three times in seven years and each reset lands on a fresh baseline; there is no official national learning trend line. These are mean item-success rates on four-option multiple-choice papers and are NOT headcount ratios - they must never be differenced against ASER, which reports the share of children clearing a fixed threshold. The guessing floor is 25 per cent and no chance-corrected score is published anywhere.

The published score is conditioned on attendance and the conditioning is nowhere documented. ASER's school visits put daily attendance in government primary schools at 72.4 (2018) to 75.9 (2024) per cent.

Values are approximate because the earliest editions are dated only by cover year, and because the entire AISHE report archive was re-uploaded to a new host in June 2025, so original publication metadata is no longer recoverable from file paths.

title: University Grants Commission gross budget provision, actuals

source.name: Notes on Demands for Grants, Department of Higher Education, Union Budget 2024-25, 2025-26 and 2026-27 editions

breaks.note: In FY2013-14 to FY2015-16 the Department's demand had no separate 'Central Universities' head at all: the UGC line, then 9,000 to 10,000 crore, carried the maintenance grants UGC passed through to central universities. After the abolition of the Plan/Non-Plan distinction from FY2017-18, 'Grants to Central Universities' became its own line - 16,146.11 crore in BE FY2025-26. The apparent halving of 'the UGC budget' between 2015 and 2018 is overwhelmingly a reclassification, not a cut.

First year in which UGC's provision is split between the Consolidated Fund of India and the Madhyamik and Uchchatar Shiksha Kosh, the education-cess fund. Gross and net now diverge by roughly 29 per cent because of MUSK routing, so reporting gross where the source reports net, or the reverse, produces a spurious step change.

points.note: Actual.
Actual. BE for this year was 5,360.00 and RE 6,409.00. Last year for which a gross figure is published: from FY2024-25 the demand shows the Consolidated Fund component only.

caveat: THE CIRCULATING CLAIM IS ARITHMETICALLY TRUE AND MATERIALLY MISLEADING. 'UGC budget slashed from 5,360 crore to 2,500 crore' compares Budget Estimate to Budget Estimate and takes the FY2024-25 figure as the Consolidated Fund component alone; the gross provision that year was 4,500 crore. The correct statement is that UGC's gross provision fell from 6,324.12 crore (Actual FY2023-24) to 4,500 crore (BE FY2024-25), a cut of about 29 per cent rather than 53 per cent, and had recovered only to 5,783.23 crore by BE FY2025-26 - still below the FY2023-24 actual in nominal terms, before any inflation adjustment. THE SERIES STOPS AT FY2023-24 DELIBERATELY. The FY2024-25 Actual published in the demand, 3,678.47 crore, is the Consolidated Fund component and not a gross figure; carrying it here would put a net point under a gross title and manufacture a 42 per cent fall. It is declared as an absence instead, and the gross figures for that year exist only as estimates.
notes: The substantive funding-model change is visible in the same accounts: HEFA appears first as an equity injection (Actual FY2017-18 250 crore, BE FY2018-19 2,750 crore) and then, from BE FY2019-20, as dedicated 'Interest under HEFA Loan' and 'Repayment of Principal of HEFA Loan' sub-lines under each institutional head - roughly 1,693 crore of HEFA debt service budgeted in BE FY2025-26 from a standing start six years earlier. Infrastructure capital that was formerly a grant is now a loan carried on the institution's books, with the debt service a claim on the same demand that funds the institutions. The FY2024-25 gross Actual is not carried: see the absence. A point on a different basis is not admissible under a title that names the basis, which is the same discipline the three GDP regimes are held to.

title: Literacy rate, persons aged 7 and above

source.name: Census of India Primary Census Abstract 2011 (final); NSS 75th Round Report No. 585; Periodic Labour Force Survey Annual Report 2025, Table 7

breaks.note: Instrument change within one definitional family. 2001 and 2011 are complete enumerations by the Census; 2018 and 2025 are sample surveys (NSS 75th Round, July 2017 to June 2018; PLFS, January to December 2025). The criterion is essentially identical across all three - a person who can both read and write a simple message with understanding in at least one language, asked of a household informant with no test administered - so they are one definitional family, but a sample cannot do what an enumeration does.

points.note: Census 2001, on the provisional basis.

CANONICAL. Computed directly from the Registrar General's own Primary Census Abstract: 763,638,812 literate persons over an age-7-plus denominator of 1,046,339,724. Males 80.88, females 64.63. The figure that appears in ministry documents, international compendia and the press is the PROVISIONAL 74.04, released 31 March 2011; splicing provisional-2011 to any later survey embeds a spurious 1.06-point step.
NSS 75th Round. Rural 73.5, urban 87.7, male 84.7, female 70.3. The report warns of itself that 'the survey was not designed to provide estimate of households and population'.
PLFS 2025, the latest measurement. Rural 77.4, urban 89.0, male 87.5, female 74.9. At the 5-plus frame it reads 80.1.

denominator: Persons aged 7 and above. Children aged 0-6 are excluded from the denominator entirely rather than counted as illiterate, which is why this is called the effective literacy rate - for Census 2011 the denominator is 1,046,339,724 rather than the full population of 1,210,854,977. Moving to a 15-plus frame costs about 4.7 points: Census 2011 reads 74.04 at 7-plus on the provisional basis and 69.30 at 15-plus.
caveat: IT IS ASKED, NOT TESTED. The enumerator or interviewer poses the question to a household informant, frequently about other members; no reading or writing task is administered at any point in the Census, NSS or PLFS. A literate person here is a person someone said was literate. Where both methods have been run on the same respondents the gap is material: NFHS-3 (2004-05) found 69 per cent self-reported against 63.4 per cent when required to read a test card, and a 1991 re-contact exercise found over 10 per cent of below-primary-educated persons reported literate by informants were illiterate when individually contacted. Never place this on an axis with ASER: reading a Standard II text is a different construct and a harder test than the national literacy statistic.
notes: Long series, all Census: 1951 18.33, 1961 28.3, 1971 34.45, 1981 43.57, 1991 52.21, 2001 64.83, 2011 74.04 provisional. Critical footnote: 1951, 1961 and 1971 use age 5-plus and 1981 onward use 7-plus; 1981 excludes Assam and 1991 excludes Jammu and Kashmir. Two official instruments are deliberately NOT carried in this series. CAMS 2022-23 gives 81.6 per cent at 15-plus but its rule is looser - for anyone ever enrolled in formal education, completing pre-primary or Class I is definitionally literacy and 'no test of the ability was performed'. NFHS-5 gives 71.5 per cent of women and 83.2 per cent of men but on a restricted 15-49/15-54 frame whose biases do not cancel. And the UNESCO Institute for Statistics series for India is a spliced patchwork of three different Indian surveys switching instrument between adjacent years - 76.32 (2022, PLFS), 81.70 (2023, CAMS), 78.16 (2024, PLFS) - a rise and fall that is demographically impossible for a stock variable, so any trend drawn through it measures instrument turnover, not learning.

unmeasured.what: A complete enumeration of literacy since 2011
unmeasured.why: Census 2021 was never fielded. The intent notification S.O. 2681(E) of 16 June 2025 supersedes S.O. 1455(E) of 2019 and sets Census 2027 with a reference date of 1 March 2027; House Listing Operations were in month five of six on 1 August 2026, Population Enumeration - which is where the literacy question sits - is not yet notified, and the gazette notification defining the Census 2027 literacy question does not yet exist. Literacy HAS been measured recently on a sample basis; what is missing is the enumeration. A sample gives no sub-district granularity (every district- and block-level literacy plan runs on 2011 geography), no small-group disaggregation at fine geography, and no population denominators - surveys give rates, the Census gives the counts of illiterate persons that programmes are sized against. By publication this will be a 16-to-18-year interval, the longest since the Indian census series began in 1881.
unmeasured.wouldFill: Population Enumeration under Census 2027, provisional results plausibly Q2 2027 and final about 2029 on the 2011 precedent

unmeasured.what: A measured national literacy rate from the ULLAS/NILP programme
unmeasured.why: ULLAS publishes counts, not a measurement. The Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Assessment Test is administered only to registered non-literate learners who were taught under the scheme and chose to sit - a self-selected, taught, pre-registered cohort with no population denominator - so its 89.6 per cent pass rate is what an end-of-course assessment yields and cannot be converted into a literacy rate. Goa was declared 'fully literate' on 30 May 2025 against a nationally prescribed 95 per cent benchmark while the same PIB release concedes PLFS puts Goa at 93.60 per cent, on the strength of Goa's own survey.

title: Children in private schools under RTE section 12(1)(c) for whom reimbursement is claimed
caveat: THIS IS NOT AN ADMISSIONS SERIES AND IT HAS NO DENOMINATOR. It is a cumulative headcount of children across Classes I-VIII in schools for which reimbursement is claimed, not annual fresh admissions, and no seats-available figure accompanies it. A second official-derived national series compiled from the same Project Approval Board pipeline gives 3,604,082 / 3,473,922 / 2,950,342 for the same three years - a divergence of up to 1.95 million children in one year. Neither can be treated as authoritative without reconciling them. The denominator is null because it is not established, and it is not established because the quantity it would require does not exist as an official statistic.
notes: The only genuine national seats-versus-filled measurement ever made was the DISE-based exercise for 2012-13 and 2013-14: a fill rate of 21.5 per cent in 2012-13 and 29.0 per cent in 2013-14, on about 21.1 lakh seats available and 6.1 lakh filled. Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh alone accounted for 320,000 of the 610,000. Everything after that is state-by-state, patchy and denominator-inconsistent. Central co-funding of section 12(2) reimbursement began in 2014-15, the first year of T1, not under the UPA.

unmeasured.what: A national series of seats notified against seats filled under section 12(1)(c)
unmeasured.why: No such series is published and the Government of India does not maintain one. Worse, the figure the Ministry labels 'total number of seats' is demonstrably a lagged reimbursement headcount: for Karnataka, the seats figure for year Y equals exactly the Project Approval Board approved reimbursement headcount for year Y minus 1, for three consecutive years, which is why seats equalled admissions perfectly for 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 - a hundred per cent fill rate by construction rather than by achievement. Any figure the Government labels 'seats' should be treated as a reimbursement-claim headcount until proven otherwise, and no national fill-rate series can be built on Ministry data.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A UDISE+-based count of section 12(1)(c) seats notified per school, which the DISE-based 2015 exercise showed is constructible

unmeasured.what: How much section 12(1)(c) money actually reached schools
unmeasured.why: The Ministry states plainly that 'the Central share is released to State/UTs based on approved funding pattern and not intervention wise'. The Centre therefore does not know, and cannot report, how much money reached schools under the provision. Approval is not release and release is not payment to schools.

points.note: 1,455.95 crore approved against 2,062.84 claimed.

denominator: The amount claimed by States in their Annual Work Plan and Budget, as tabled in Lok Sabha Unstarred Question 2160 of 05.08.2024, source PRABANDH. Only 17 States and UTs appear in the table at all.
caveat: APPROVAL IS UPSTREAM OF RELEASE, WHICH IS UPSTREAM OF PAYMENT TO SCHOOLS. The cumulative shortfall of 2,451.39 crore across the five years is a FLOOR on the central-approval gap, not a measure of what schools are owed, and the Centre does not account for section 12(1)(c) money separately once released. Two structurally different failure modes are averaged together here: Uttar Pradesh was approved a tenth of its claim, while Karnataka claims exactly 200.00 crore every single year and is approved almost exactly that - a flat ceiling, which is the 20-per-cent-of-AWP&B cap binding rather than a demand-driven figure.
notes: Reimbursement is funded under Samagra Shiksha at a per-child cost notified by the State, for Classes I-VIII, subject to a maximum ceiling of 20 per cent of the State's approved Annual Work Plan and Budget - a ceiling stated identically in 2021 and 2024 with no evidence it was ever raised. States pay first from their own funds and then claim. Pre-primary admissions under the provision are outside central reimbursement altogether even though many states admit at pre-primary, and Chhattisgarh's extension of the benefit to Classes IX-XII since 2019 is funded entirely from state funds. The upstream blockage is the per-child cost norm: asked in September 2020 and again in July 2022 whether it would standardise the calculation, the Ministry gave a word-for-word identical answer both times - states have flexibility, and '12 States/UTs have revised their per child cost since 2014-15'. The count did not move in 22 months.

points.note: '17 States and UTs have started admissions.' The same reply records that all except Telangana, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh had notified the eligible disadvantaged groups - so the gap between notifying and admitting is the size of the paper-compliance problem.
'19 States/UTs are admitting children under Section 12(1)(C).' Lakshadweep has no private unaided schools.

denominator: 36 States and Union Territories.
caveat: ROUGHLY HALF THE COUNTRY HAS NEVER OPERATED THE PROVISION, on the Ministry's own count, fourteen years after the Act commenced. And in December 2024, asked directly for 'the details of the States/UTs that have failed to implement RTE Act along with the reasons for non-implementation', the Ministry gave no list and did not answer the question, replying only that education is in the Concurrent List. That refusal is itself a datum.
notes: An independent classification for February 2023 lists as non-implementing: Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Kerala, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Punjab, Sikkim, Telangana, West Bengal, Jammu and Kashmir and Puducherry, with Manipur and Ladakh notifying under process and Karnataka and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands implementing partially. It is internally inconsistent between 18 and 20 implementing jurisdictions, so treat 18-20 as the honest range. Manipur started implementation only in 2024-25, confirmed at T1, with a first claim of 0.34 crore. Jammu and Kashmir is the sharpest case: the RTE Act was not in force there before August 2019 because the state assembly never passed it under Article 370 - and extension of the Act after the reorganisation did not produce implementation, with the disadvantaged groups still unnotified as of September 2020 and the jurisdiction listed non-implementing in 2023. Minority institutions are exempt from the Act entirely following Pramati (2014), which structurally shrinks the seat base.
